content: The tree marigold, also known as the Mexican tournesol, Mexican sunflower, or Nitobe chrysanthemum (scientific name Tithonia diversifolia), is a plant species belonging to the Asteraceae family. It is now distributed across tropical and subtropical regions, including Central America, Southeast Asia, and Africa. Depending on the region, this plant can be either annual or perennial, typically growing to a height of two to three meters. It has upright stalks that are sometimes woody, resembling shrubs. The flowers of the tree marigold are orange in color. It is widely believed that the plant originated in Central America or Mexico, which is reflected in its common names. Symbolism and Uses In Japan, during the late Meiji Period, the tree marigold was introduced as an ornamental plant, although it was rarely cultivated there. The plant has a distinct bitter taste and was historically used to induce fever as a means of combating poisoning, though it was not employed for direct medicinal purposes. There is also a historical account suggesting that the species was introduced to Japan by Nitobe Inazo, which is why it is referred to in Japanese as the Nitobe chrysanthemum (ニトベギク; Nitobegiku). In Mexico, the plant is traditionally used to treat sprains, bone fractures, bruises, and contusions. In Southern China, it is utilized for the treatment of skin diseases such as athlete's foot, as well as for conditions like night sweats, hepatitis, jaundice, cystitis, and as a diuretic. In Taiwan, the tree marigold is sold in herbal medicine markets, where it is infused to support liver function. Additionally, the tree marigold is recognized as the provincial flower of Mae Hong Son Province in Thailand.
